Accuse
ac-cūze´
v. (to charge with a crime or fault; rendering Hebrew lashan, Aramaic akal qartsin, Greek kategoreo)
From Latin accusare, from ad causam, to call to account, to bring to the cause. An accusation is a formal summons to answer.

Biblical Definition

Accuse is a courtroom word that Scripture watches with suspicion, because of who does most of the accusing. Proverbs warns against it in ordinary life: “Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty” (Pro 30:10) — the accuser risks the guilt he tried to transfer. John the Baptist forbids it to soldiers with power to make it stick: “accuse any falsely” is set beside violence and extortion (Luk 3:14). The Gospels show accusation as the settled method of the Lord's enemies, who watch Him beside a man with a withered hand “that they might accuse him” (Mar 3:2) — a human being reduced to bait. And when the accusations finally come, “the chief priests accused him of many things: but he answered nothing” (Mar 15:3). Behind them all stands the original: Satan, “the accuser of our brethren… which accused them before our God day and night” (Rev 12:10), and the announcement that he is cast down.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines accuse as to charge with, or declare to have committed a crime, either by plaint or complaint, information, indictment or impeachment — and to blame or charge with a fault.

expand to see more

ACCUSE, v.t. To charge with, or declare to have committed a crime, either by plaint, or complaint, information, indictment, or impeachment.

2. To charge with a fault; to blame; to censure.

Their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another. Rom. ii.

It is followed by of before the subject of accusation.

Key Scripture

Rev 12:10 — "And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night."

Mar 3:2 — "And they watched him, whether he would heal him on the sabbath day; that they might accuse him."

Pro 30:10 — "Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty."

Luk 3:14 — "And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages."

Modern Corruption

Accusation industrialized as a public form of entertainment and power, while the believer's standing answer to it — that the Accuser is cast down and an Advocate pleads — goes unused.

expand to see more

Public accusation is now a currency. It is cheap to make, expensive to answer, and rewarding to whoever makes it first, and Scripture's warnings read as if written for it. Proverbs 30:10 attaches a boomerang to the practice — the accuser is found guilty — and Mark 3:2 exposes the worst feature of accusation culture: the men watching Jesus were not interested in the man with the withered hand at all. He was an occasion. Whenever a real sufferer becomes useful chiefly as evidence against someone, Mark 3 is being re-enacted.

The pastoral half of this entry matters more. Many believers live under an accusing conscience that never rests, and Revelation 12:10 names the source: an accuser who works day and night. The answer is not to argue the charges, most of which are true, but to plead an Advocate. Christ answered nothing before the chief priests because He was accepting the charge on behalf of others. The accused Christian therefore has a defence he did not construct and cannot lose.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lashan (H3960), to use the tongue, slander, accuse; Aramaic akal qartsin, literally to eat the pieces of a man — the idiom in Dan 3:8; Greek kategoreo (G2723), to speak against in court.

expand to see more

Hebrew lashan (H3960) — to slander with the tongue, accuse; the verb of Pro 30:10.

Aramaic akal qartsin — to eat the pieces of, a vivid idiom for malicious accusation; used of the Chaldeans who accused the Jews (Dan 3:8).

Greek kategoros (G2725) — an accuser, prosecutor; in Rev 12:10 it is the title of Satan, cast down.

Usage

"“The accuser of our brethren… which accused them before our God day and night” — and he is cast down."

"“That they might accuse him” — a suffering man reduced to evidence."

"“Accuse not a servant unto his master… and thou be found guilty” — the charge rebounds."
